newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals-Cobalt price seen down on summer lull.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals-Cobalt price seen down on summer lull.

text.p: Cobalt prices are expected to fall fall slightly due to the sluggish summer holiday season but may bounce back towards the end of the year due to a supply shortfall, Japanese traders said on Thursday.
High-grade cobalt was being quoted at $22.50-23.00 per pound and low-grade metal at $19.20-19.50.
"Business is becoming slow due to the summer holiday season. End-users here are not actively covering cobalt at the moment," a cobalt trader at a major trade house said.

Sources close to Gecamines, the state cobalt producer in the Democratic Republic of Congo, said recently the country was reeling from the after-effects of a seven-month civil war, with its output this year set to fall to well below 4,000 tonnes.
"Given the possible supply problem, such as from Gecamines, cobalt prices are likely to gain further. But sharp rises from the current levels look unlikely at the moment," he said.

Traders also said they were cautious ahead of a U.S. cobalt industry meeting on Thursday. The Defence National Stockpile Center has called a meeting to discuss how to sell strategic stockpiles of the metal following legal battles with Minor Metals Inc.
Chinese traders said that cobalt prices were seen falling slightly on the summer slump, with Chinese ingot now being quoted C&F basis Rotterdam at $19.20 per lb.
One Chinese trader said she has not seen price indications for Chinese cobalt in recent weeks, despite reports of some consumer demand in Europe.
A European source said his company did not bother with the Chinese material as it came with too many quality, packing and delivery problems.
Antimony was still in good supply, traders in Hong Kong and southern China said, with shipments of the local material moving out of the southern island of Hainan to Europe and Southeast Asia.
Chinese antimony was indicated at $1,900 a tonne C&F Rotterdam, a little lower than the London indication, ex-Rotterdam for any source, late last week of $1,950/2,000.
Vanadium supply was tight, with prices pushed up to $4.05/4.15, according to buyers' offers, a trader said.
One Shanghai producer of vanadium pentoxide and ferro-vanadium was said to be extremely hard-pressed for slag supply, but could not be contacted for details.

Panzhihua, a big Chinese producer of vanadium-titanium-iron concentrate and the country's biggest producer of slag, was rumoured to be closed for summer maintenance, but this was denied by sources at the factory in Sichuan province.
